problem: The sentence 'Two forces on the same rigid body can be replaced by their vector sum at any point on the common line of action after sliding' is wrong in general. Two forces usually do not share a line of action; what they share is an intersection point. Adding them 'at any point on a common line' only works for collinear forces, and for non-collinear forces the resultant must act at the intersection of the two lines of action, otherwise the moment is not preserved. A student will try to add non-collinear forces at a convenient point on one of the lines and get the wrong resultant position.
fix: Two forces on a rigid body are slid along their own lines of action until they meet at the point where the two lines intersect. The two forces are then replaced by their vector sum acting at that intersection point (or by a resultant plus a couple if the lines are parallel). Only for collinear forces is the 'common line of action' language correct.

problem: 'Keep the perpendicular distance to any moment centre the same' is listed as an action step, but the student does not do anything to keep it the same. It follows automatically from sliding along the line, and listing it as a step suggests the distance must be adjusted by hand.
fix: Move it out of the action list and state it as a check: 'The perpendicular distance from any moment centre to the line of action is unchanged by the slide, so M_O = F d is unchanged.'

where: Section 1, definition of line of action
problem: 'The straight line through the force vector' is loose. The force vector is drawn as an arrow from the point of application, so a student may think the line is only as long as the arrow, or that it passes through the middle of the arrow rather than through the point of application.
fix: Say: the line of action is the infinite straight line along which the force acts; it passes through the point of application and runs in the direction of the force arrow.
